newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: New Bangui clashes kill 10 people, French hurt.
newsitem.headline: New Bangui clashes kill 10 people, French hurt.

text.p: Fresh clashes in the Central African Republic capital killed at least 10 civilians on Saturday and wounded dozens, including French nationals hurt when a stray mortar shell hit their embassy compound, witnesses said.
Witnesses and hospital sources put Saturday's death toll during a second day of clashes between African peacekeepers and disaffected soldiers at at least 10.
The deaths took to at least 14 the number of people killed in two days of fighting, including one Senegalese peacekeeper.

French Ambassador Jean-Marc Simon told a French television network that mortars had apparently been fired from Camp Kassai, a base for former army mutineers, towards a camp of forces loyal to President Ange-Felix Patasse.

"As these people are unfortunately very bad shots... the shells fell scattered around the upper part of the city of Bangui and two hit the French embassy compound," he told the La Chaine Info television by telephone from Bangui.
"One of the staff will have to be repatriated to France...because he has shrapnel in his lungs."
Of the seven injured in the compound, five were French nationals and two staff from the Central African Republic.

The African force, deployed under a January 25 peace deal, has been touted as a model for a force to restore peace to Brazzaville, capital of the neighbouring Congo Republic where similar ethnic and political clashes broke out on June 5.
The Red Cross and the peacekeeping force said Friday's clashes killed a peacekeeper, a child and two women.
Saturday's clashes focused on suburbs where the dissident soldiers, principally from the southern Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba, enjoy popular support.

Residents in areas loyal to the disaffected soldiers, who have yet to rejoin their units after three army mutinies in under a year, said Chadian peacekeepers conducted house-to-house searches and accused them of killing anyone who resisted.
One report spoke of shells from Patasse's presidential guard hitting the mutineers stronghold of Ouango, near Camp Kassai.
A spokesman for the dissident soldiers, many of whom have already rejoined their units under the deal, said earlier they had told their men not to attack but to remain on the defensive.
Friday's incident was the first since a failed June 13 attempt to reintegrate mutineers from the paramilitary gendarmerie into their units under the January peace plan.
Mali's respected former military leader, Amadou Toumani Toure, who brokered the deal, was expected back in Bangui.

Mutinies in April and May 1996 began as protests over pay but became a movement to topple Patasse, a northern civilian elected in 1993. The third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.
Peacekeepers' spokesman Captain Lamine Gueye said Friday's shooting erupted when peacekeepers intervened to stop a group of former mutineers holding up a private vehicle.
Parfait Mbaye, a spokesman for the disaffected troops, said there had been no attempted hold-up and the peacekeepers had tried to disarm former mutineers returning to their base.

French troops, in the country under a defence pact, restored order after the latest mutiny and handed over to the peacekeepers. The African force includes soldiers from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo.
